subject: Banking
title: The Revolving Door
description: A quick win: understand The Revolving Door.

hook.text: Goldman Sachs alumni have served as US Treasury Secretary, World Bank president, and heads of central banks globally.

buildup.text: The revolving door means bankers move into government, write regulations, then return to banking.

discovery.text: Henry Paulson went from Goldman CEO to Treasury Secretary.

twist.text: Defenders say banking expertise is needed in government. Critics say it ensures regulation always favors Wall Street.

climax.text: When regulators come from Wall Street and return to it, independence is always in question.

punchline.text: Goldman to Treasury and back again. The door keeps revolving.

quiz.question: What is the 'revolving door' in banking?
options: Bankers moving between Wall Street and government regulatory positions

details.summary: The revolving door refers to the flow of personnel between investment banks and government regulatory agencies, where former bankers become regulators and former regulators join banks, raising concerns about regulatory capture.
details.whyItMatters: When regulators come from and return to the industry they oversee, they may be reluctant to impose strict rules on future employers. This dynamic has shaped financial regulation for decades and fuels public distrust.
takeaways: Former Goldman Sachs executives have held top government positions worldwide
Regulatory capture occurs when regulators favor the industry they oversee
Cooling-off periods attempt to limit conflicts but are often insufficient

faq.question: What is the most famous example of the revolving door?
faq.answer: Hank Paulson left Goldman Sachs as CEO to become Treasury Secretary in 2006, then oversaw the bank bailouts that saved Goldman from potential collapse in 2008. His former firm received billions in government support under his watch.

faq.question: Are there rules preventing the revolving door?
faq.answer: Cooling-off periods prohibit former regulators from lobbying their agencies for one to two years. But these are easily circumvented, and the cultural familiarity between Wall Street and Washington persists regardless of formal restrictions.
